planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Tripartite won the ADS Wister Award in 1999 for its reliable garden performance across many US regions.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Tripartite is a split-corona (collar) daffodil that opens up to three bright lemon-yellow blooms per strong stem, giving an unusually floriferous, orchid-like display for a standard-size cultivar. Because the open, flattened corona lies close to the petals, it reads as a solid wash of color from a distance, which is part of why it earned the Wister Award for outstanding garden performance. Leave foliage to yellow naturally after bloom to recharge the bulbs for next year.

common_name: Monal Daffodil (Golden Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Red-Orange Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Monal received the ADS Wister Award in 2000 for consistent, vigorous garden performance.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and about as far apart in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Monal, a Grant Mitsch hybrid, produces large, well-formed blooms with rounded golden-yellow petals set off by a deep red-orange cup, giving strong color contrast in mid-spring beds. The sturdy stems hold the oversized flowers well above the foliage, making it a reliable choice for cutting as well as garden display. Allow the clump to bulk up undisturbed for several years before dividing.

common_name: Golden Aura Daffodil (All-Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Ruffled Rim)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Golden Aura won the ADS Wister Award in 2001 for dependable garden performance.

directions: Set bulbs 4-6 inches deep in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Golden Aura carries widely overlapping, bright yellow petals behind a large, bell-shaped cup in a matching gold tone with a softly ruffled rim, so the whole flower reads as a single warm color from a distance. Its sturdy habit and clean, long-lasting bloom made it a standout in regional garden trials across the country. Group bulbs in drifts for the strongest visual impact in a spring border.

common_name: Fragrant Rose Daffodil (Scented Pink-Cupped Large-Cupped Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Fragrant Rose won the ADS Wister Award in 2005 for its later bloom and good form.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Fragrant Rose opens later in the season than most large-cupped daffodils, with a reddish-pink cup brushed with yellow and green against a pale perianth, and carries a genuine soft rose scent rather than the usual faint daffodil fragrance. Its late timing helps stretch the daffodil season into the point where many earlier cultivars have already finished. Plant near a path or patio where the fragrance can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Dainty Miss Daffodil (Fragrant White Jonquilla Daffodil with Green Eye)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Dainty Miss won the ADS Wister Award in 2006 and performs well as far south as zone 9.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. This Grant Mitsch jonquilla hybrid bears pure white flowers with a small, slightly greenish eye and a sweet fragrance noticeable from several feet away, making it a favorite for cutting and containers as well as garden beds. Its compact, intermediate size and heat tolerance let it naturalize well in warmer parts of the South, unlike many jonquilla types bred for cooler climates. Mass several bulbs together for the best scent and visual effect near entries or seating areas.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Camelot was one of several cultivars honored with the ADS Wister Award in 2007.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Camelot produces rounded, solid-yellow flowers with a deep, flared cup edged in a finely serrated rim, giving a tidy, formal look that holds up well on the show table and in the border alike. It blooms reliably in mid-spring and is sturdy enough for cutting without staking. Plant in bold groups rather than singly, since the uniform gold color reads best in a mass.

common_name: Brackenhurst Daffodil (Golden Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Reddish-Orange Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Brackenhurst won the ADS Wister Award in 2008.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to half shade. Brackenhurst pairs golden-yellow petals with a bold, funnel-shaped cup in deep reddish-orange, giving strong two-tone contrast on tall, sturdy stems. It is a vigorous grower that multiplies readily, making it a good choice for naturalizing in larger drifts as well as formal beds. Deadhead spent blooms to keep plantings tidy, but let the foliage die back fully before removing it.

common_name: Crackington Daffodil (Golden Yellow and Orange Double Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Crackington won the ADS Wister Award in 2009 for garden-worthy double flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Crackington is a double daffodil whose ruffled, layered petals mix golden yellow with streaks of frilled orange, giving a shaggier, more textured bloom than single-form cultivars. Because double daffodils can be heavy-headed after rain, a site with some wind protection helps keep the stems upright through the bloom period. It makes a long-lasting cut flower and a lively accent among earlier, simpler-flowered daffodils.

common_name: Dreamlight Daffodil (Historic White Small-Cupped Daffodil with Pink-Orange Rim)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; this 1934 Guy L. Wilson heirloom won the ADS Wister Award decades after its introduction.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Bred in Northern Ireland by Guy L. Wilson in 1934, Dreamlight carries a wide, flat, champagne-white eye rimmed with a narrow band of orange flushed pink, a color combination that still looks fresh among modern cultivars. Its long garden history and proven vigor across many regions are exactly what later earned it the Wister Award. Because it is an older, less widely produced heirloom, source bulbs early in the fall ordering season from specialty daffodil suppliers.

common_name: Blushing Lady Daffodil (Soft Yellow Jonquilla Daffodil with Pink-Flushed Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Blushing Lady, a Brent Heath hybrid, won the ADS Wister Award in 2022.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by Brent Heath of Brent and Becky's Bulbs, Blushing Lady carries two to three soft yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers per stem with a halo at the base of the cup that develops a pink flush as the bloom matures and ages. Its late-season timing extends jonquilla-type bloom further into spring than earlier multi-flowered cultivars. Plant it near walkways or outdoor seating so its fragrance and color shift can be enjoyed at close range.

common_name: Delibes Daffodil (Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Delibes, a pre-1950 Dutch introduction, won the ADS Wister Award in 2023.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Delibes, raised by F. Rijnveld and Sons in the Netherlands before 1950, pairs broad greenish-yellow petals with a lightly ribbed cup that shades from yellow to orange at a frilled mouth. Decades after its introduction it still proved vigorous and consistent enough across US regions to earn the Wister Award. It is a strong naturalizer, so let clumps multiply undisturbed for a bolder show each spring.

common_name: Bantam Daffodil (Historic Intermediate Greenish-Yellow Daffodil with Orange-Rimmed Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; this pre-1950 Barr and Sons heirloom won the ADS Wister Award in 2024.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Bred in England by Barr and Sons before 1950, Bantam is an intermediate-size daffodil with rounded, blunt, brilliant greenish-yellow petals surrounding a smooth to lightly ribbed orange cup with a broad yellow base. Its compact scale and late bloom make it a useful bridge between the main daffodil flush and the perennials that follow. Long garden history combined with proven reliability across regions earned it the Wister Award nearly a century after its introduction.

common_name: Pacific Rim Daffodil (Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange-Red Rimmed Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Pacific Rim won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2000, recognizing a standard daffodil of exceptional show-quality merit bred by an American hybridizer.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Pacific Rim bears clear yellow petals behind a very shallow, bowl-shaped cup edged with a crisp band of orange-red, a flat, saucer-like form that sets it apart from deeper-cupped daffodils. Its clean color and show-quality form on strong stems made it a repeat favorite on the exhibition table as well as in the garden. Plant in groups for the best display of its distinctive flat-cupped silhouette.

common_name: POPS Legacy Daffodil (White and Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; POPS Legacy, a William Bender hybrid, won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2004.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Bred by William Bender, POPS Legacy is an early-season trumpet daffodil with a broad, heavy-textured white perianth set off by a lightly ribbed, cylindrical bright yellow trumpet as long as the petals. The strong contrast between pure white and clear yellow gives it presence even planted singly, though it reads best in groups. Its early bloom and good substance make it a dependable opener for the daffodil season in beds and show collections alike.

common_name: Conestoga Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Apricot-Orange Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Conestoga, a 1985 William Bender hybrid, won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2002.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Conestoga, raised by Pennsylvania hybridizer William Bender, pairs a smooth white perianth with a flat, bright apricot-orange crown that softens toward orange-yellow with a hint of green at the center as it ages in warm weather. Its well-closed, rounded petals give the flower a neat, show-ready form that also holds up in the garden. It is a reliable mid-season bloomer for beds that mix large-cupped cultivars of contrasting color.

common_name: Pink Silk Daffodil (White Trumpet Daffodil with Apricot-Pink Corona)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Pink Silk won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2008.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Pink Silk is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil whose white petals frame a long, flaring trumpet in a soft apricot-pink, a shade that intensifies slightly as the flower matures in cool spring weather. Its compact stature compared to many white-and-pink trumpets makes it useful toward the front of a border or in containers. Grow it alongside deeper-colored large-cupped cultivars to let its pastel trumpet stand out.

common_name: Lemon Silk Daffodil (Pale Lemon Cyclamineus Daffodil with Reflexed Petals)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Lemon Silk won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2014.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Bred by Grant Mitsch and refined by Richard and Elise Havens, Lemon Silk carries well-reflexed, pale lemon-yellow petals swept back from a long, narrow trumpet that fades to nearly white at its base. The elegant, swept-back form typical of its Cyclamineus heritage gives it a lighter, more graceful look than bulkier large-cupped types. It clumps up well over time, making larger, more striking drifts in subsequent seasons.

common_name: Mesa Verde Daffodil (Yellow-Green Daffodil with Spring-Green Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Mesa Verde, bred by Robert Spotts, won the ADS William G. Pannill Award in 2015.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Mesa Verde, bred by California hybridizer Robert Spotts, falls outside the standard divisions with a greenish-yellow perianth and a cup carrying an unusual clear yellow-green tint that gives the flower's center a fresh, spring-green glow rarely seen in daffodils. This distinctive coloring made it a novel addition to exhibition collections and a conversation piece in the garden. Plant where the unusual green cast can be viewed up close rather than from a distance.
